ety.text: Latin posseder. Vulgar Latin potēre Old French pooir Anglo-Norman poerbor. Middle English power English power From Middle English power, poer, from Old French poeir, from Vulgar Latin potēre, from Latin posse, whence English potent. Compare French pouvoir. Displaced the native Old English anweald.

senses.d: The ability to do or undergo something.
ex: He has lost the power to speak.
If it is spirits who have power to suffer, it seems they would also have active powers to think and will.

senses.d: The ability to coerce, influence, or control.
The ability to affect or influence.
ex: the power of the written word

senses.d: The ability or authority to control, govern, command, coerce, etc., such as in a legal, political or business sphere.
ex: He's nominally president, but he does not have any real power.
In the face of expanding federal power, California in particular struggled to maintain control over its Chinese population.

senses.d: The people in charge of legal or political power, the government.
A strong or influential nation, company, or other such body.
ex: In the 19th century, Britain and France were major colonial powers.
Britain is no longer the maritime power that it once was.

senses.d: An army, a military force.
Physical force or strength.
ex: He needed a lot of power to hit the ball out of the stadium.

senses.d: Designating one who does something forcefully or on a large or grand scale.
ex: She's a power shopper; she knows all the best deals.
This high-spec computer is ideal for power users.

senses.d: The production or flow of energy providing means to do work; energy per time unit.
ex: The power to haul the train is supplied by two huge locomotives.

senses.d: To provide power for (a mechanical or electronic device).
ex: This CD player is powered by batteries.

senses.d: To hit or kick something forcefully.
To enable or provide the impetus for.
To move or advance with great force or speed.
Impressive.
ex: Check out the POWER Mee Rebus & Lontong in this newly established Nasi Padang coffee shop at Market Street Carpark.
Their performance is very the Power!

senses.d: Used as a cheer to express support

From Middle English poudre, pouder, pouldre, borrowed from Old French poudre, poldre, puldre, from Latin pulverem, accusative singular of Latin pulvis (“dust, powder”). Doublet of pulver. Compare pollen (“fine flour”), polverine, pulverize.

senses.d: The fine particles which are the result of reducing a dry substance by pounding, grinding, or triturating, or the result of decay; dust.
ex: Let me goe grin'd their Bones to powder ſmall, […]

senses.d: Cocaine in powder form (as opposed to crack).

senses.d: To use powder on the hair or skin.
To turn into powder; to become powdery.

To depart suddenly; to "take a powder".
